title: Async/Await Under the Hood
description: Coroutine state machines, epoll and kqueue, Node.js libuv, Python asyncio, Kotlin structured concurrency, and backpressure in async systems.

segments.text: Async/await looks like magic: you write code that reads sequentially but handles thousands of concurrent operations without threads. Under the hood, it's a state machine, an event loop, and OS-level I/O multiplexing. Understanding these internals is critical when your async system starts dropping requests under load.

When you write an async function with two await points, the compiler transforms it into a state machine with three states. State zero runs code before the first await. State one runs code between the awaits. State two runs code after the second await. Each await suspends the function, saving local variables, and the event loop can run other work.

The event loop is the runtime's heartbeat. It checks for completed I/O operations, runs their callbacks or resumes their coroutines, then checks again. Node.js runs a single event loop on one thread. Python asyncio runs a single loop per thread. The critical rule: never block the event loop. A single blocking call stops ALL concurrent operations.

Under the event loop sits OS-level I/O multiplexing. Linux uses epoll, macOS uses kqueue, Windows uses IOCP. epoll monitors thousands of file descriptors and returns only the ones that are ready. A single thread can monitor 100,000 connections. The old select syscall scanned all file descriptors linearly — epoll uses a callback mechanism that's O(ready events).

Node.js uses libuv, a cross-platform async I/O library. Network I/O uses epoll/kqueue on the event loop thread. But file I/O and DNS lookups use a thread pool of four threads by default. This is why reading a large file can block other file operations. Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE for I/O-heavy Node.js applications, but know that this doesn't help network operations.

A Node.js service suddenly shows 10-second response times for all requests. CPU is at 100 percent on one core. A developer added a JSON.parse call on a 50MB payload. Since JSON.parse is synchronous and runs on the event loop thread, it blocks all other requests for the 200 milliseconds it takes to parse. One blocking call, total service degradation.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you handle parsing a 50MB JSON payload in Node.js without blocking the event loop?

segments.text: Python's asyncio has a critical limitation: the GIL. The Global Interpreter Lock means only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. Asyncio works around this for I/O-bound workloads because awaiting I/O releases the GIL. But CPU-bound work in an async function blocks the entire loop. Use ProcessPoolExecutor to offload CPU work to separate processes.

Kotlin's structured concurrency solves a fundamental problem: leaked coroutines. In unstructured async, launching a coroutine and forgetting about it means it runs forever if the parent completes. Structured concurrency ties coroutine lifetimes to scopes. When a scope completes, all child coroutines are cancelled. This prevents resource leaks that accumulate over days in production.

Async systems can accept work faster than they can process it. Without backpressure, memory grows unboundedly as pending tasks queue up. Node.js streams have highWaterMark that pauses the producer when the buffer fills. Go channels block the sender when full. Reactive Streams in Java have explicit request-based flow control. Ignoring backpressure causes OOM kills in production.

Cancellation in async systems is hard. When you cancel an HTTP request handler, what about the database query it started? The file it's writing? Proper cancellation propagates through the entire call chain. Go uses context.Context with cancel. Python uses Task.cancel. Without proper cancellation, cancelled requests continue consuming resources, wasting database connections and CPU.

Compare three approaches to handling 10,000 concurrent connections. Thread-per-connection: 10,000 threads, 80 gigabytes of stack memory, massive context switch overhead. Async event loop: single thread, 10,000 connections on epoll, minimal memory. Thread pool plus async: best of both, N threads each running an event loop, like Tokio in Rust.
segments.thought_prompt: Why does Tokio use a multi-threaded runtime with work-stealing instead of a single event loop like Node.js?

segments.text: Async/await is a compiler trick that turns sequential-looking code into state machines driven by event loops. The power comes from OS-level I/O multiplexing. The danger comes from blocking the event loop, ignoring backpressure, and leaking coroutines. Master these internals, and you'll know exactly why your async service is slow before looking at a single metric.
